notes.6: Many candidates didn’t seem to understand what a tally was so left that column blank or had the frequency there. Those who had the frequency there often then had a probability or a percentage in the last column. There were the usual arithmetic inaccuracies also.
notes.8: (a) This question was well answered. b) Many correct answers were seen to this part. The most common error was to cube rather than cube root the number.
notes.9: There were many correct answers seen but also many candidates scored just 1 mark for a partial factorisation, particularly for 2 x (2 x – 4 y ). A few wrote –4 xy as their answer.

notes.17: A significant number of candidates calculated simple interest. Many calculated the compound interest but lost the final mark through premature rounding. Some just gave the interest as their answer. Others spoilt their method having successfully found 646 by adding 600 back on or by multiplying 646 by 3.
notes.18: Many candidates scored full marks on this question. Others lost out through a lack of working. Candidates must understand that when a question says ‘you must show all your working’ that they will not be awarded marks for the correct answer without working. Other than this, the main loss of a mark was due to not cancelling to the simplest form.
notes.21: (a) This part was not well answered with 6 w being the most common error. Other incorrect answers were 1 and 0. 0 3 (b) Few correct answers were seen to this part, with 2 x or 2 x or even x (5–3) given as the answer. (c) This part was correct more often than parts (a) and (b) . However a large number of candidates were not able to calculate the indices and several scored 1 mark for 15 y , while others ignored the indices and gave 15 as the answer. 3 4 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2017
notes.2a: Some candidates gave diameter but the majority had correctly named the radius.
notes.2b: The term chord was less well known.
notes.3a: This was well answered with the majority of candidates giving the correct answer.
notes.4a: This was not very well answered since most candidates did not show the small hand far enough past 3. Almost all wrote the big hand at 9. Many candidates showed the time 2.45.
notes.4b: This was generally correct although a small number of candidates used incorrect time notation e.g.15 45 pm. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2017
notes.5a: Many candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was 5370 from rounding to the nearest ten.
notes.5b: This part was also well answered. Common errors were 42.3 and 42.34780.
notes.7a: Most candidates were able to work out the pattern of this sequence. Possibly the hardest part was working out 4–10.
notes.7b: This part was less well answered with some candidates starting with 0 and giving the answers 5, 8 and 11.
notes.10a: This question was not well answered. Several candidates missed or incorrectly entered the x co-ordinate. A significant number did not attempt the question.
notes.10b: Many candidates had not realised the coefficient of x was the gradient from the equation given, with 4x or –6 or blank responses seen. Some tried drawing a grid with the line on and calculating the gradient. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2017
notes.11a: Many correct answers were seen. However several candidates gave the answer 26 from poor use of a calculator.
notes.11b: This part was mostly correct with the most common error being 9.
notes.11c: Most candidates had the correct answer for this part.
notes.12a: Most candidates understood this use of algebra and 180° in a triangle was well known, although some found the angles in terms of x rather confusing and didn’t understand how to tackle the question. 7 x + 6 x + 5 x = 18 x so x = 18 and 7 x + 6 x + 5 x = 360 were common errors.
notes.12b: Many correct answers were seen in this part but the follow through was rarely applied as many who did not understand part (a) were also confused here. Almost all who got part (a) correct also were successful with part (b) .
notes.14a: Many candidates were able to give the correct answer, although some just stated 4.1–2.7 without carrying out the calculation.
notes.14b: Many candidates were able to give the correct answer, although some hadn’t listed all ten numbers. Others made errors in the addition, with 30.87 and 30.4 being common incorrect totals.
notes.15a: Many candidates were able to correctly identify either of the two required answers. 81 was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.15b: Many of those candidates who found the correct value lost marks by leaving their answer as 3 × 7 × 10 or 2 × 3 × 5 × 7. Others confused HCF and LCM with the answer of 3 being seen often. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2017
notes.16a: Many candidates were unable to answer this question. Some repeated 5 as the answer.
notes.16b: Many candidates did not realise that multiplication of equations was not necessary. However, many did reach the correct answers even if they did more work than necessary.
notes.19a: Many candidates were able to correctly plot the points. Errors were largely due to incorrect use of the scale.
notes.19b: The answer to this part was generally correct.
notes.19c: The majority of candidates were able to draw a line within the allowed tolerance. There were some candidates who thought the line of best fit had to go through the origin.
notes.19d: Many candidates were able to use their line of best fit. Errors were as in part (a) due to incorrect reading of the scale.
notes.20a: Many candidates had realised the need to use Pythagoras’ theorem and could apply it successfully. A significant number of candidates lost a mark for giving the answer 8.9 rather than 8.91.
notes.20b: Those who realised that trigonometry was needed usually gave the correct answer. A small number used cosine or tangent rather than sine. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2017
